Revised assessment using the SLOOS as reference:
- The statement’s caution is warranted. The July 2020 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey indicates broad-based tightening of lending standards and terms across C&I and CRE loans, as well as consumer credit (credit cards and autos), alongside weaker loan demand in most categories. Banks cite a deteriorating economic outlook and reduced risk tolerance, with expected worsening in credit quality—especially for SMEs, CRE (lodging/retail), and lower-score consumer borrowers. While low rates boosted mortgage demand (particularly refi), standards tightened notably for many mortgage segments (e.g., jumbos), implying uneven pass-through.
- These SLOOS findings suggest that, despite improved market functioning and supportive financial conditions, bank intermediation remains a headwind: tighter standards can constrain credit availability and amplify downside risks to activity and employment, keeping inflation pressures subdued near term.
- Policy mitigants remain meaningful. The FOMC’s average inflation targeting and explicit lower-for-longer guidance, continued Treasury/MBS purchases, and standing liquidity/market backstops help anchor expectations and support market-based credit. However, SLOOS implies that the bank credit channel will recover only gradually, tempering the pace of healing.

Net: Compared with an assessment anchored only in market functioning, the SLOOS points to tighter bank credit supply and softer demand, tilting the outlook more negative despite strong policy support.
